assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on the magic-wavelength idea, moved timekeeping to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and are the clearest case of a new measurement technique changing what can be observed (relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches, a candidate redefinition of the second). Originality, clarity and breadth of consequence are all high, and it fits the tradition of the 2005 comb and 1989/2012 precision-spectroscopy prizes.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice trapping and led the Sr demonstrations; Ye's group brought the clocks to the lowest systematic uncertainties and many-body (Fermi-degenerate) operation. A two-person prize is clean, though contributions from other groups (e.g. Yb and Hg lattice clocks, the Lemonde and Gill groups) could be argued, and I cannot verify every priority claim from memory.
assessment.maturity: Mature: many independent clocks worldwide, routine comparison over fibre links, and international metrology bodies are acting on them. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to bundle in ion clocks or other contributors with a wider configuration.
Priority details for the lattice proposal versus early experimental demonstrations are from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms gave inertial sensing (gravimetry, gyroscopes, measurement of G and of alpha) of exceptional precision and opened a new class of instruments. It is an experimentalist's discovery in the strictest sense and has real applications, for example in geophysics and navigation, with fundamental-physics reach.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard made the first atom interferometers with material gratings, Bordé supplied the theory and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, and Kasevich (with Chu, who is not in the credited names and is already a laureate) demonstrated the light-pulse atom interferometer. The credit is plausible but entangled with earlier prizes, so a three-person split needs care.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with commercial and field instruments and large-scale gravitational-wave and equivalence-principle experiments in progress. The long-baseline fundamental-physics applications are still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 1997 and 2001 prizes (laser cooling, condensates) and Chu's absence from the credited list complicate attribution.
The most dramatic tests (e.g. gravitational-wave detection with atoms) are not yet demonstrated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed states and their use to beat the standard quantum limit now sit inside the Advanced LIGO and Virgo detectors, which is a case where a quantum-optics idea directly improves a landmark measurement. The concept is clear, deeply tied to measurement precision, and has demonstrated impact.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied the 1981 proposal for squeezed-light interferometry; Kimble led the first experimental generation of squeezing (in the Slusher-era work, where Slusher and Yurke are not credited here); Schnabel and Mavalvala drove practical implementation in gravitational-wave detectors. Four credited names for a maximum of three places makes the choice contestable, and I picked Mavalvala for the implementation in LIGO.
assessment.maturity: Mature for the physics and for GEO600/LIGO deployment, though the 2017 prize for LIGO already covers the main gravitational-wave success.
uncertainties: Whether a squeezing prize is seen as too close to the 2017 gravitational-wave prize.
Which of Kimble, Schnabel and Mavalvala best represents the decisive contribution is unresolved; Slusher and colleagues are not among the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single NV centres in diamond gave a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a nanoscale magnetometer, thermometer and field sensor with uses from nanoscale NMR to biology. It has opened a field and enabled much downstream work, which matters to me.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko demonstrated single-NV optical detection and spin control; Lukin's group drove the sensing, quantum-register and many-body extensions. The three-way split is credible, but other groups (e.g. Awschalom, Hanson) have large contributions that the credited list omits.
assessment.maturity: Mature as a field with many independent groups and early commercial devices. The ultimate practical impact is still unfolding.
uncertainties: Omitted contributors such as Awschalom and Hanson may be viewed as comparable.
Sensing impact beyond proof-of-principle is not yet settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller 1995 proposal for ion-trap quantum gates and the Blatt group's gate and algorithm demonstrations established the leading hardware platform for quantum computing and simulation. The theory-plus-experiment pairing is the sort of result I respect, but the ion-trap control methods themselves partly overlap with the 2012 Wineland prize.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the decisive proposal and Blatt made leading experimental demonstrations; Wineland (a laureate) and Monroe also carry large experimental credit, and Blatt's inclusion over them could be disputed.
assessment.maturity: Mature in terms of the proposal and early gates; the application to scalable computing is still developing, and commercial systems are only beginning.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize, and whether committee would want a broader quantum-computing prize.
Experimental credit split with Wineland and Monroe.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ti:sapphire gain media and Kerr-lens mode locking became the workhorse of ultrafast optics and enabled femtosecond spectroscopy, frequency combs and attosecond science. This is an enabling instrument with a very wide footprint, comparable to the chirped-pulse amplification prize in kind.
assessment.attribution: Moulton demonstrated and developed the Ti:sapphire laser, and Sibbett's group demonstrated self-mode-locking by Kerr-lens. The two names fit a clean award, though others in the Sibbett group (Spence, Kean) and in industry are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature; the technology is decades old. The only issue is whether recognition now is still of interest after the 1999, 2005, 2018 and 2023 prizes closely related to it.
uncertainties: Likelihood that the committee sees the topic as already largely recognised through adjacent prizes.
Co-credit for the first self-mode-locking observation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices provide controllable quantum many-body simulators and realised the Mott transition and Hubbard models with in situ microscopy. The measurement capability, single-site resolution and tunable interactions are impressive, and the theoretical proposal gave the field its direction.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch et al.) made the lattice Hubbard proposal; Bloch and Greiner realised the superfluid-Mott transition, and Esslinger reached the fermionic Hubbard regime. Greiner is the fourth name and excluded by my choice, which is debatable.
assessment.maturity: Mature as a platform, though the scientific outcomes (a clear answer to an open condensed-matter question) are still emerging.
uncertainties: Not yet clear that quantum simulators have solved an open problem.
Choice among four credited names is contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics reached the mechanical quantum ground state, sideband cooling and entanglement of macroscopic oscillators, which extends quantum control to massive objects and underpins ultra-sensitive force and displacement measurement. It sits on the measurement-limit theme I care about.
assessment.attribution: Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg are central to cavity optomechanics; Cleland's group did the first quantum ground-state demonstration of a mechanical resonator. Other groups (Lehnert, Painter, Schwab) are not credited, and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits may bear on attribution.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. Quantum-limited measurements and sensing applications are real but practical uses are still few.
uncertainties: Closeness to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum phenomena.
Other leading groups are not among the credited names.
